The terminal holds its breath. For three agonizing seconds, my screen is a static void of black. Then, the command line spits out a string of neon green text. 

`HANDSHAKE ACCEPTED.`
`PROTOCOL_BLUE DEPLOYED.`
`DIAGNOSTIC TUNNEL OPEN.`

I’m in. 

Protocol_Blue worked exactly as Moth implied. Croft’s automated defenses saw my mirrored payload, recognized it as a priority self-audit, and quietly opened a backdoor through the firewall directly into Sector 9. I slip through the digital crack before the system can realize it just invited a ghost into the machine.

Sector 9 isn't a standard database. It’s a subterranean vault of raw, uncompiled data. There are no neat folders, no labeled directories. Just thousands of encrypted data blocks floating in the dark. The "fragments." 

Croft was paranoid enough to shred the Erebus master file into a thousand pieces, scattering them across this air-gapped subnet. Any single fragment looks like garbage code. Meaningless. Harmless. 

But I have the blueprint. 

I write a rapid-assembly script, using the mirrored architecture of Moth’s original message as the cipher. I tell my script to look for the jagged edges of the code—the orphaned variables, the incomplete loops—and stitch them together. 

I hit execute. 

On my center monitor, a progress bar crawls forward. The terminal window becomes a blur as my script pulls the fragments from the dark and slams them together. 

`ASSEMBLING FRAGMENT 001... [OK]`
`ASSEMBLING FRAGMENT 042... [OK]`
`ASSEMBLING FRAGMENT 899... [OK]`

Bit by bit, the shadow of Erebus takes shape. It’s not a ledger. It’s not a decentralized network. 

It’s a weapon. 

The final fragment slots into place, and the compiled master file decrypts. The truth hits me like a physical blow to the chest. 

Erebus isn't a trapdoor to hide Croft's wealth. It’s a cascading zero-day worm designed to target SCADA systems—the industrial control networks that run the physical world. Water treatment plants, nuclear cooling towers, power grids, automated logistics hubs, and undersea fiber-optic relays. 

Croft isn’t trying to hack the global economy. He’s planning to flatline it. 

I scroll frantically through the compiled schematics. The code is designed to trigger a synchronized, global hardware failure. It will overload transformers, sever communication uplinks, and wipe the redundant backups of the world's major financial institutions. It will plunge the planet into a literal and digital dark age. *Erebus.* The shadow between Earth and Hades. 

And Croft? He’s sitting in a self-sustaining, heavily armed fortress in the Alps, sitting on billions in hard assets and precious metals. When the lights go out and the world burns, the man with the only working flashlight becomes a god. 

A red warning light starts flashing in the corner of my screen. 

`SYSTEM ALERT: UNAUTHORIZED COMPILATION DETECTED IN SECTOR 9.`

They found me. Protocol_Blue’s diagnostic window is closing. Croft's red-team AI is waking up, hunting for the anomaly. 

I don't have time to dismantle the worm from here. The core execution protocol is hardwired to a physical server inside the Alpine compound. I rip the compiled Erebus schematics to my encrypted drive, sever the connection, and nuke my routing proxies, burning the bridge behind me just as Croft's security slams the door shut. 

The monitors go dark again. 

I sit in the silence of my safehouse, the weight of the encrypted drive heavy in my hand. I know what Erebus is now. I have the map. But knowing the bomb exists isn't enough; someone has to cut the wire. 

My cover as Elias Thorne is still intact. Croft knows someone breached Sector 9, which means he’s going to be more desperate than ever for a threat auditor. He’s going to invite me right through his front gates. 

I grab my coat,
